title: David shouting at God
hookLine: David shouting at God — anger is allowed
carry: you can say anything to him
tomorrow: why the symbol is an execution device

cards: Anger at a person. Anger at a life. Sometimes, anger at God, or the universe, or whoever runs things.

It can seem like the one feeling nobody brings to church, where everyone shows up polite. Now open the middle of the Bible, and there's a whole book of people who didn't. "How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?"
That's not a complaint about God. It's a complaint to God, out loud, and it's scripture.

teach.b: The Psalms. A hundred and fifty poems, the songbook of ancient Israel, still prayed by Jews and by Christians. The name comes from Greek, psalmos, a song sung to a plucked string.
The Hebrew title is Tehillim: praises. Tradition ties many of them to David, the shepherd boy who became king; the headings put his name on about half, and scholars debate how many he actually wrote.

teach.h: SO MUCH OF IT IS COMPLAINT.
teach.b: For a book called praises, a great deal of it is complaint. Scholars call these laments, and there are a lot of them.
That first line asks how long four times in two verses. Another psalm opens with a cry you'll hear again tomorrow, from the cross: "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?"
And one psalm ends in darkness, with no comfort at all. If prayer has ever felt like talking to the ceiling, that one is in the book too. These weren't hidden away.
Many carry headings addressed to the chief musician: songs to be sung. Laments often have a shape.

teach.h: FIRST THE HONEST PART. THEN A TURN.
teach.b: First the honest part: where are you, this isn't fair, I'm going under. Then, often, a turn. The how long psalm ends by saying the singer has trusted in God's mercy and will sing again.

teach.h: YOU DON'T HAVE TO BE POLITE.
teach.b: In these songs, the anger doesn't have to be cleaned up first. It's the way in.

how: Christians sing and pray the Psalms in church services and at home. In monasteries, and in the daily prayer of some churches, the Psalms are prayed in order over a set cycle.

games.q: you're a singer in ancient Israel, and you feel forgotten by God. what goes into the songbook?
o: only the praise. keep the complaint private.
games.why: "how long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? for ever?" it went in the book, and people still sing it.

practice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe. Think of something you're upset about.
Not a crisis, but something real, something you've been keeping polite about. Silently, say it straight. No softening.
How long. Why. This isn't fair.
If you pray, you can say it to God, the way the Psalms do. If you don't, say it to the quiet. Then breathe, and notice what's left once it's been said.
You don't have to fix anything.

wordCard.voice: The Psalms. A hundred and fifty songs, with praise and complaint side by side. Seventeenth word.
